own_scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

similar_scenes.desc: Nevermind de Nirvana (noviembre de 1991) llega al número uno el 11 de enero de 1992 y acaba con el reinado del lite metal. Los medios abrazan a Kurt Cobain y Eddie Vedder, las radios crean formatos «alternativos», la gran emisora de metal de Los Ángeles, KNAC, se vende en 1995 y MTV cancela Headbangers Ball en 1996; hasta Kerrang! se abre a la nueva moda, y los críticos, que crecieron con el rock universitario, ven por fin validado su gusto. El grunge no es metal aunque comparte la guitarra y la voz fuerte: alterna partes duras y suaves, canta el dolor y la desesperación, viste de tienda de segunda mano e identifica a la generación X con los débiles, frente al poder y el placer del metal («Somos pesados, pero no heavy metal», dice Krist Novoselic). Hacia 1998 el alternativo está moribundo.

podcast.title: Origin of Term - Mark Arm (1981)
podcast.body: In 1981, Mark Arm of Mr. Epp and the Calculations used the word "Grunge" in a letter to the alternative weekly "Desperate Times" to describe his band's "pure noise" sound. This marks the first known appearance of the word in print as a descriptor for a specific music style from the American Pacific Northwest, although the term had existed in American slang to denote something repulsive. "This is the first known appearance of the word Grunge in print as a description for a certain style of music from the American Pacific Northwest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Deep Six Compilation (1985)
podcast.body: The "Deep Six" compilation, released in the fall of 1985, was a pivotal record that provided focus and identity to the then-fractured Seattle scene. Featuring bands like The Melvins, Soundgarden, and Green River, it allowed the Pacific Northwest community to hear a cohesive representation of their regional sound for the first time. "That came along in the fall of 1985 when several local bands contributed songs to a compilation called Deep Six."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution Post-1988
podcast.body: The evolution of grunge became clearer from 1988 onwards, with many publications from Sub Pop being officially considered grunge. "a partir de 1988 la evolución del granch es mucho más fácil porque ya en su pop tenemos muchas publicaciones ya que las conseguimos casi oficialmente granch."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Mainstream Acceptance Delayed (1988-Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In 1988, the music world was largely unprepared for the grunge sound and attitude, as hair metal was still dominant and alternative rock remained marginalized. Seattle itself was considered an obscure location. However, within approximately two and a half years, grunge successfully took root, thanks to the rise of bands like Soundgarden, Nirvana, Pearl Jam, and Alice in Chains. "But within about two and a half years, Grunge took root, thanks to groups like Soundgarden and Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: British Journalists' Early Excitement - Early 1989
podcast.body: The first professional journalists to become excited about the Seattle grunge scene were British, not American. This started in early 1989. "Now, many people have forgotten that the first professional journalists to really get excited about the Seattle grunge scene were not American. They were British."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Early UK Popularity - 1989
podcast.body: Grunge was "all the rage in the UK" in 1989, even while most of North America remained unaware of it, largely due to early coverage by British music papers like Melody Maker and NME. "The result was that while most of North America was still unaware of grunge, it was all the rage in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Mainstream Jump Post-1989
podcast.body: After 1989, particularly with the release of Nirvana's *Bleach* and later albums by Pearl Jam and Alice In Chains, the grunge movement transitioned from Sub Pop to Geffen and became widely known globally. "Justo después ya todo el movimiento granch, saldría de su pop a Giffen y la parte más andegranada un pura se quedaría en su pop."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Cultural Storm Example (1990-1996)
podcast.body: Grunge is cited as an example of a "perfect cultural storm," with its period of significant impact and influence spanning from 1990 to 1996. "Think of Grunge from 90 to 96."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Origins in 1990 Recession
podcast.body: The recession that began in 1990 is directly linked to the emergence of grunge music. "The next recession came in 1990, which, as we all know, began grunge and the intense alt rock that we saw early in that decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Rise in US (1990)
podcast.body: The beginnings of Grunge in the US in the spring of 1990 contributed to rock's quick resurgence, alongside Madchester in the UK. "There was the rise of Madchester in the UK and the beginnings of Grunge in the US."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Late 1991 Emergence and Teenage Engagement
podcast.body: Grunge "hit in late 1991" and was a defining genre for teenagers, who "sucked up" music from bands like Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Alice in Chains, and Soundgarden during their formative years. This period was crucial for their musical identity formation.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: MTV Genesis (1991)
podcast.body: The music video for Nirvana's "Smells Like Teen Spirit" in 1991 is widely recognized as the video that ushered in the entire Grunge era. Its raw, energetic visuals, filmed in a high school gymnasium with real fans destroying the set, became an iconic representation of the genre. "And who could forget the video that ushered in the whole Grunge era in 1991?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Pre-Mainstream Status During Singles Filming (1991)
podcast.body: During the filming of *Singles* in early 1991, the Seattle grunge scene was "basically unknown to people outside the extreme Pacific Northwest." Major label signings for bands like Soundgarden hadn't yet registered broadly, and key bands like Pearl Jam and Nirvana were still in their nascent stages, highlighting the scene's pre-explosion status. "At the time, the Seattle Gren scene was basically unknown to people outside the extreme Pacific Northwest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Holy Trinity of Albums (1991)
podcast.body: The "holy trinity of grunge albums" comprises Pearl Jam's "Ten," Nirvana's "Nevermind," and Soundgarden's "Badmotorfinger," all released in 1991. These three records provided a diverse selection of new guitar rock for listeners and were instrumental in launching grunge into the mainstream. "this record became the first of the holy trinity of grunge albums. It's 10 from Pearl Jeff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singles Movie and Soundtrack (1992) Impact
podcast.body: The release of the movie *Singles* and its soundtrack in 1992 occurred in a world where alternative and specifically grunge "ruled everywhere." The film, with its music of the moment and cameos from bands like Pearl Jam and Alice in Chains, along with songs played widely on radio and in clubs, played a crucial role in making the "grunge tent even bigger." "And together with the movie, singles made the grunge tent even bigger."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peak Popularity and Market Impact (1993)
podcast.body: In October 1993, Grunge was at its absolute peak, and Pearl Jam's fanatical sales for their album "Vs." served as a "giant wake-up call" that "New Rock," "Alt Rock," "alternative music," or "modern rock" had undeniably "arrived." "Now Grunge, if you remember, was at its absolute peak and fanaticism of Pearl Jam was especially, well, fanatical."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2

podcast.title: Spread to Britain (Early 1993)
podcast.body: In early 1993, the spread of American Grunge was causing an "operative crisis" for British music and contributing to the decline of the Manchester Sound. "British music was about to inter-operative crisis thanks to the spread of American Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Context in 1994
podcast.body: For a young grunge fan in 1994, the historical context of Woodstock was as remote and unfamiliar as grunge might be to someone born after Kurt Cobain's death today. "Kurt, Grunge, and everything that happened in the early 1990s is as remote and unfamiliar to you as Woodstock was to a young Grunge fan in 1994."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline After Kurt Cobain's Death - April 1994
podcast.body: Following Kurt Cobain's death in April 1994, grunge and the entire American alt-rock scene rapidly became "yesterday's news," entering a long, slow decline. This created a void that Britpop was well-positioned to fill. "When Kurt Cobain died in April 1994, Grunge in the entire American alt-roxene was suddenly yesterday's news and started a long, slow decline."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Fatigue and Decline by 1994
podcast.body: By early 1994, the original Grunge movement was experiencing fatigue, with an proliferation of derivative "Grunge-like" and "Grunge-Lite" bands, while many of the authentic Grunge bands began losing momentum. This decline was exacerbated by public weariness with Kurt Cobain's complaints and personal drama, and the underwhelming sales of Nirvana's *In Utero*. "By the beginning of 1994, the original Grunge thing was looking very close to being beaten to death. The number of derivative bands really began to multiply. Too many Grunge-like bands and Grunge-Lite bands as many of the actual Grunge bands were starting to lose momentum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Waning Influence (1994)
podcast.body: Although still popular in 1994, grunge appeared to be declining, with alt-rock fans beginning to seek out new sounds. "Grunge, although still very big in 1994, seemed to be on the wane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Control (1995)
podcast.body: By 1995, with only a few exceptions, the grunge genre had largely transitioned from its independent roots to come under the control of major record labels. "By 1995, but with a few exceptions, Grunge had largely come under the control of the majors."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline by 2000
podcast.body: By the turn of the millennium, "the grunge heroes had either broken up, checked out, moved on, or died," contributing to Alt Rock's perceived dead end. "The grunge heroes had either broken up, checked out, moved on, or died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: "Alt Rock with Training Wheels"
podcast.body: Grunge was described as "alt rock with training wheels" because its "different yet familiar approach to traditional guitar rock" served as an accessible entry point that "lured people in" and inspired millions to explore deeper into the alternative music scene. "Not only did they make great music, but instead of this, it was also alt rock with training wheels that lured people in with its different yet familiar approach to traditional guitar rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Alt-Rock with Training Wheels"
podcast.body: Grunge bands not only created great music but also served as "Alt Rock with training wheels," successfully luring people into the alternative music scene. Their "different yet familiar" approach to traditional guitar rock drew millions into the "alternative nation," inspiring them to explore deeper into alt-rock and beyond.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Holy Trinity" of Albums
podcast.body: The foundation of grunge was formed by three pivotal albums released in the fall of 1991: Pearl Jam's "Ten" (August 27, 1991), Nirvana's "Nevermind" (single August 27, 1991, album September 24, 1991), and Soundgarden's "Badmotorfinger" (October 8, 1991). "Three records formed the foundation of Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Aging of Generation X and Artists
podcast.body: As the Gen Xers who championed grunge grew up and moved on, so did the artists. This, coupled with events like Kurt Cobain's death, band issues (Smashing Pumpkins), hiatuses (Alice in Chains), and breakups (Soundgarden), alongside Pearl Jam's deliberate distancing, contributed to the scene's decline. "Besides, the Gen Xers who made grunge when a wad's grew up, got jobs, started families and basically moved on. And so did the artists who made the scene possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alternative Music with Training Wheels
podcast.body: For many, Grunge served as an accessible entry point into alternative music, often described as "alternative music with training wheels," which then led listeners deeper into a subculture that had long existed outside the mainstream. "For many, Grunge was alternative music with training wheels. Those who liked what they heard were invariably led deeper into a culture that had existed outside the mainstream for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: American Alt Rock Contribution
podcast.body: Grunge is identified as one of the main American contributions to Alt Rock in the 1990s, alongside the punk rock revival. "If the main American contributions to Alt Rock were grunge in the punk rock revival, and if the UK's was Britpop, ours was Can Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artists' Aging
podcast.body: Many prominent grunge artists from the 1990s are now in their 50s and 60s, with some having passed away, highlighting the passage of time since the genre's peak. "All the legendary grunge artists are in their 50s and 60s, if not dead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 3: (80-71)

podcast.title: Becoming the New Classic Rock
podcast.body: Today, grunge has, "in some ways," become the "new classic rock," with acts from that era still being promoted and remaining popular. "Well, in some ways, grunge has become the new classic rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Biggest Sound of the Decade
podcast.body: Grunge was identified as "the biggest sound of the decade" in the 1990s, responsible for ripping a hole in the music space-time continuum and allowing alternative sounds to invade the mainstream. "Then along came Grunge, the biggest sound of the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Book About Grunge and Government
podcast.body: Chris Novoselic wrote a book titled "of Grunge and Government" in 2004, reflecting his political interests. "Chris's big thing is Electoral Reform, and in 2004 he wrote a wafer-thin book called of Grunge and Government."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakthrough on US Charts
podcast.body: The summer of 1991 marked the period "when Grunge began to break on the US charts," with Alice in Chains being the first Seattle band to achieve significant radio play for the genre with "Man in the Box." "the summer of 91 was when Grunge began to break on the US charts."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Bridging Punk and Metal
podcast.body: Grunge, spearheaded by bands like Nirvana and their peers, played a crucial role in the early 1990s by closing the "gap between punk and old school metal," as artists like Kurt Cobain openly cited metal bands as influences. "With Nirvana and all their grunge peers, the gap started to close between punk and old school metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Opposition
podcast.body: The success of grunge and its related subgenres, particularly in North America, became a "problem for certain people in the UK." This perceived American dominance of the music scene led to a British backlash and the emergence of Britpop. "But I will tell you this, Grunge and its cousins were certainly a problem for certain people in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Resistance and "Musical Imperialism"
podcast.body: The popularity of grunge in the UK sparked a backlash from many in Britain who viewed it as "musical imperialism" from the colonies, which they felt "must be stopped." This sentiment helped fuel the rise of homegrown Britpop. "How could this music from the colonies be taking over? It's musical imperialism. It must be stopped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Catalyst for Record Label Pivots
podcast.body: The unexpected sales success of grunge, particularly Nirvana's Nevermind, prompted record labels to drastically "pivot" their strategies. This shift initiated the "Grunge Gold Rush," as labels aggressively sought to sign more alternative rock acts. "So this caused the record labels to pivot... And so began the Grunge Gold Rush."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Categorization of Stone Temple Pilots
podcast.body: Upon hearing songs like "Plush," many listeners and critics were quick to categorize Stone Temple Pilots as a grunge band, or worse, a "blatant Pearl Jam rip off," despite Scott Weiland's personal aversion to the label and his attempts to differentiate the band's style. "When most people first heard the song, they were quick to categorize STP as a grunge band or worse, a blatant Pearl Jam rip off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Centrality in the 1990s
podcast.body: In the 1990s, grunge held the "center" of the alt rock scene, providing a dominant and unifying sound that shaped the genre for the decade. This contrasts with the fragmentation of alt rock in the 2000s. "In the 90s, grunge held from the center."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Characteristics of the Sound
podcast.body: Grunge was characterized by low-tuned guitars and an anti-star image for its frontmen and women, becoming the most familiar sound of the 90s Alt Rock explosion and the genre around which all others evolved for years. "Grunge moved from being a sea of different sounds to one that centered on low-tuned guitars and anti-star frontman and women."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Codification of Alternative
podcast.body: Grunge emerged as a defining sound that codified the previously scattered alternative rock universe, providing a central point around which everything else could coalesce and organize, making Alt Rock unstoppable for a period. "But then along came something that sort of codified everything, something around which everything else could coalesce and organize."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Colin McDonald's Early Bands
podcast.body: Colin McDonald's early musical endeavors in high school included playing in "not serious" grunge bands with friends. "I started playing in like not serious like kind of punk and grunge bands in high school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Commercial Face of Alternative Music
podcast.body: Grunge became the commercial face of alternative music, providing the music industry with a much-needed boost during a recession. Its street cred combined with a consumer-friendly sound made it highly appealing. "Grunge was just what it needed. Rock with loads of street cred and a consumer-friendly sound. Grunge became the commercial face of alternative music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Community of Fury
podcast.body: The Seattle scene was not just a limited group of specific bands but a collective of generally furious people, contributing to the introspective and raw nature of the music. "no era una escena de limitada de bandas concretas, era un grupo de gente generalmente muy rabiosa."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Consigned to History
podcast.body: By the end of 1997, grunge was considered "consigned to the history books," much like Britpop and Technopop, signifying its era had passed. "Britpop was officially done, consigned to the history books, just like Grunge and Technopop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Consolidating 90s Alt Rock
podcast.body: Grunge became so big and popular in the 1990s that it consolidated and codified alt rock as almost exclusively guitar-based, narrowing the genre's sonic scope. This was beneficial for spreading the alt rock attitude globally but ultimately led to dilution and burnout by the decade's end. "Grunge was so big and so popular that it had the effect of consolidating and codifying alt rock as almost exclusively guitar based."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continuum, Not Inflection Point
podcast.body: The transition from hardcore punk or "slag" (thrash/sludge metal) to grunge was not marked by a clear inflection point. Instead, it was a gradual appearance of early bases of grunge within various rock movements of the late 1980s. "no tiene un punto de inflexión que podamos decir claramente aquí es donde termina el hardcore punk o por ejemplo el slag y empieza el sonido del granch."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Core Principles
podcast.body: The grunge movement valued authenticity, humbleness, and "street cred," actively downplaying and avoiding the concept of conventional stardom. It embraced "slacker culture" with its "apathetic egalitarianism," focusing on the people, the fans, and "real, honest music." "Gen X wanted music of their own, music made by their own people that dealt with their own issues and attitudes. And they let it be known that they valued authenticity, humbleness, and street cred."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Identity
podcast.body: Grunge transcended mere music; it was a comprehensive culture with its own rules, goals, politics, aesthetic, philosophy, and fashion sense, eventually developing its own class system. "Grunge wasn't just a type of music. It was a culture with its own rules and goals and politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline Post-Kurt Cobain's Death
podcast.body: The death of Kurt Cobain "prematurely killed any momentum Grunge had," leading to a decline in American rock and creating a vacuum that British bands quickly filled. "But Cobain killed himself. And that prematurely killed any momentum Grunge had."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Decline after Kurt Cobain's Death
podcast.body: The death of Grunge's biggest star, Kurt Cobain, in April 1994, brought the genre's momentum to "a dead stop" and shook all of North American alt-rock, creating a vacuum that Britpop was able to fill across the Atlantic. "The death of Grunge's biggest star brought all that momentum that Grunge had almost to a dead stop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline and "Well Going Dry" (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: The original grunge bands eventually "died off," and by the late 1990s, the "Grunge well basically went dry," leaving no concrete genre to replace it. This period was followed by what is described as "Dreck-like New Metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline and Rise of Intimist Music
podcast.body: The grunge era eventually "acabó con cierto modo muriendo" (ended in a certain way dying), paving the way for a new generation of artists embracing more intimate and introspective music. This shift in musical taste helped to elevate the figure of Jeff Buckley posthumously, as his pioneering intimate sound found a more receptive audience. "el gruncha acabó con cierto modo muriendo vino una nueva generación de gente como mucho más intimista."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Decline in Mid-1990s
podcast.body: Grunge's dominance began to decline around mid-1996 as Generation X aged and moved on, the artists defining the era lost momentum or disappeared, and an improving economy made the "dour sounds" of grunge less resonant. This decline paved the way for the resurgence of happy pop music. "Gen X grew up and moved on, the artists that defined the early nineties either disappeared or lost their momentum, the economy improved so the dour sounds of grunge no longer resonated as much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Defining Era of the Early 1990s
podcast.body: The early 1990s were famously "the era of grunge," dominated by influential bands such as Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Alice in Chains, The Smashing Pumpkins, and Stone Temple Pilots. These bands were known for their distinctive "slow and low" sound, often employing a "quiet loud dynamic." "Now, this of course was the era of grunge. We had Nirvana, Pearl Jam and Sound Garden, Analysis and Chains and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition and Origins
podcast.body: Grunge, a term that none of the tagged bands liked or adopted, was characterized by its fusion of "punk and new wave into hard rock and even metal." Its foundations were laid years before Nirvana, with pioneers such as Soundgarden and Green River. "What made Grunge a term by the way that none of the bands tagged as Grunge either liked or adopted was how it fused punk and new wave into hard rock and even metal."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Developed from Hardcore Punk
podcast.body: Grunge is listed as one of the genres whose development was fundamentally influenced by hardcore punk. "el granch."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Egg Punk: Explorando el lado más raro del punk

podcast.title: Diffused Origin
podcast.body: Grunge did not have a clear, distinct beginning or a simple break from previous styles like some other musical movements. It is described as a very diffuse, complex, and dispersed movement, making its precise delimitation difficult. "La música granch no es ese estilo, es un estilo muy difuso que nos cuesta mucho de limitar."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Direct Hardcore Influence
podcast.body: Hardcore is cited as an essential prerequisite for the existence of grunge, emphasizing its foundational role in the genre's development. "Honestly, no hardcore, no grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Displacement by Modern Punk
podcast.body: By 1995, modern punk, influenced by the mid-90s revival, successfully displaced grunge as the leading sound within alternative rock. "By the time we got to 1995, this modern brand of punk had displaced grunge as the top alt-rock sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Displacement of Prior Rock
podcast.body: The emergence of Grunge, along with other alt-rock, caused a "damn broke" effect, flooding the mainstream and eventually "displacing, or washing away... almost all the rock the world had known up until that time," likened to "the destruction of Atlantis." "See, when Grunge came along, a damn broke. All this alt-rock, which had existed in a parallel and separate universe, came flooding into the mainstream, eventually displacing, or washing away if you want to carry on the metaphor, almost all the rock the world had known up until that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominance and Subsequent Shift (Early-Mid 1990s)
podcast.body: Grunge, led by bands like Nirvana, became the dominant sound of alternative rock from 1991 through 1993, fusing East Coast dissonance with metallic sludge from the Pacific Northwest. However, as the genre progressed, particularly after Kurt Cobain's suicide in the spring of 1994, mainstream tastes began to shift towards "perky less-dour music," making way for more melodic and acoustic sounds. "But with Grunge getting all the attention from 91 through 93. Hoody still seemed too mellow for major labels on the hunt."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Dominance in Alt-Rock (1990s)
podcast.body: Grunge, driven by bands like Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Alice in Chains, and Nirvana, became so popular and influential in the 1990s that it "effectively became alt rock," causing the genre to coalesce around hard guitar rock and marginalize other alternative sounds. "Grunge was so big and so popular that it effectively became alt rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant North American Sound (Early/Mid-90s)
podcast.body: Grunge was the predominant North American sound in the early and mid-1990s, largely due to bands like Nirvana and Pearl Jam. "Grunge was the dominant North American sound of the early and mid-90s thanks to Nirvana and Pearl Jam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant Style (Late 1980s-Early 1990s)
podcast.body: During the late 1980s and early 1990s, Grunge music was at its peak, characterized by deeply introspective and self-focused lyrical content. Its themes often revolved around personal feelings of sadness, confusion, frustration, jealousy, and depression, embodying a predominantly internal perspective. "Estábamos en pleno a ojo de la música Grunge...un mensaje muy introspectivo, muy basado en cómo yo me siento o cómo yo sufro o cómo yo me afronto al mundo...era como todo muy de yo hacia adentro."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Poniendo en su lugar a Rage Against the Machine

podcast.title: Dominant in Early 1990s
podcast.body: Grunge was the dominant genre in the early 1990s, characterized by "guitarras tan duras tan garajeras" (such hard, garage-like guitars). This sound, exemplified by bands like Alice in Chains and Nine Inch Nails, created a challenging musical environment for artists like Jeff Buckley, whose intimate and melancholic style did not align with the prevailing trends of the time. "teníamos el grunch teníamos las guitarras tan duras tan garajeras."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Drop D Tuning
podcast.body: Drop D tuning became nearly synonymous with the grunge genre, notably employed by bands such as Nirvana, Soundgarden, Pearl Jam, and Alice in Chains. This tuning, where the lowest string is dropped from E to D, makes guitar chords sound grittier, heavier, and more powerful, especially when combined with foot pedals and overdriven amps, thus becoming a defining characteristic of the genre's sound. "Drop D not only became synonymous with grunge, Nirvana, Sound Garden, Pearl Jam, Allison Chains, but it can be heard in a lot of other songs by the Foo Fighters, Muse, Tool, Green Day, Rage Against the Machine, and dozens of others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

podcast.title: Early 1990s Dominance
podcast.body: Grunge was a dominant and "awesome" form of alternative rock in the early 1990s, alongside industrial, Manchester, and Britpop. However, its appeal faded away by the late 1990s, contributing to a sense of disillusionment in the rock scene, particularly in the wake of Kurt Cobain's suicide. "The awesomeness of the alternation of the early 1990s, with grunge and industrial and Manchester and Britpop, had faded away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Early 90s "Dude Heavy" Scene
podcast.body: When Grunge emerged in the early 1990s, it was "again very dude heavy," despite some of its figures like Kurt Cobain and Pearl Jam members being "woke-sympathetic" to feminist ideals. The scene remained "very much a boys' club," which spurred the formation of Riot Grrrl. "When Grunge came along in the early 1990s, it was again very dude heavy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 90s Dominance
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, grunge music became immensely popular, invading the commercial rock scene of the United States. Nirvana was considered "the jewel in the crown" of this movement. "la música gran se había invadido todo lo que era la escena rock comercial de Estados Unidos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Bands
podcast.body: Early grunge bands included Nirvana, Alice In Chains, Pearl Jam, and Soundgarden. "Las primeras bandas de granch como Nirvana o Alice In Change como Pearl Jam, Sound Garden."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Early Development by BamBam
podcast.body: The band BamBam, fronted by Tina Bell, was doing their "grunge thing" in Seattle as early as 1983, predating the widespread recognition of the genre by several years. Tina Bell is considered one of its inventors. "Tina was a Black woman who fronted a very grungy sounding band from Seattle called BamBam, and they were doing their Grunge thing in 1983, a couple of years before that sound really began to catch on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Seattle Sound Codification
podcast.body: Soundgarden's initial EPs, "Screaming Life" and "FOP," released on Sub Pop Records, were pivotal in codifying the distinct "Seattle sound," which combined "punk aggression, metal doom, sludgy guitars, and here and there, pop hooks." "Subpop released Soundgarden's first two EPs, Screaming Life and Thop, which helped codify the Seattle sound."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Eddie Vedder as Grunge Icon
podcast.body: Eddie Vedder, frontman for Pearl Jam, is recognized as a grunge icon, known for his serious social, political, and environmental views, a stark contrast to his early childhood modeling career. "Now, of course, Eddie is a grunge icon with serious social, political and environmental views."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence in Early 1990s
podcast.body: In January 1993, grunge was identified as a significant and growing music phenomenon, alongside the rise of Lollapalooza. This burgeoning popularity led radio station management to embrace an alternative format rather than switching to country music. "Grunge was happening. Lola Palusa was a thing..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence in Early 90s
podcast.body: The grunge era of the early 90s saw the term "alternative" being used to describe a new generation of music that descended from punk and new wave, marking a shift in its definition from label origin to aesthetic and sensibility. "by the time we got to the grunge era of the early 90s, alternative was being used to describe a new generation of music that had descended from punk and new wave and not from Led Zeppelin and the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence in the Late 1980s/Early 1990s
podcast.body: In the late 1980s, grunge was still a few years away from its widespread popularity, with hair metal being the dominant genre. The emergence of grunge would significantly shift the musical landscape. "Now you gotta remember that this is the late 1980s, hair metal was big and grunge was still a few years away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Quality
podcast.body: Grunge is ultimately "destined to endure" because, like other influential sounds, "good music is good music." "Grunge is destined to endure like so many other sounds that came before it. Because, well, like I said, good music is good music, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution to Mainstream
podcast.body: Throughout 1992 and 1993, Grunge "gradually evolved into the defining alternative rock sound," transitioning from the cutting edge to a mainstream phenomenon. "throughout 1992 and 93, Grunge gradually evolved into the defining alternative rock sound, shifting from the cutting edge to the mainstream."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Exclusion of Pioneers from History
podcast.body: Despite BamBam's early contributions, Tina Bell and her band were never given the deserved credit and are almost completely absent from the official history of grunge. "Tina and BamBam were Grunge before anyone even started using that word, but Tina and the band were never given the credit they deserve. In fact, they're almost completely expunged from the history of Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Explosion of the Early-Mid 90s
podcast.body: The "grunge explosion" of the early to mid-1990s was a pivotal period during which this underground form of rock and roll dramatically rose to prominence, ultimately surpassing and replacing many mainstream rock acts. Bands such as Nirvana, Soundgarden, and The Smashing Pumpkins became highly influential during this era. "Eventually, thanks mainly to the grunge explosion of the early mid-90s, this underground form of rock and roll overtook and replaced most of the mainstream rock acts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Female Response to Male Dominance
podcast.body: Riot Grrrl bands largely sprang up as a direct "female response to Grunge," due to the perception that the male-dominated music offered "no room for us." This spurred women to create their own space and sing about their own issues, directly challenging the existing paradigm. "Riot Girl bands sprang up largely as a female response to Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fender Twin Reverb in Grunge
podcast.body: The Fender Twin Reverb amplifier, known for its clean sound, surprisingly found use in the grunge era, which was largely characterized by distortion. Kurt Cobain notably used a Twin Reverb on Nirvana's "Bleach" album, demonstrating its unexpected versatility. "The amp even found use in the Grunge era, which seems a little weird given that Grunge was all about distortion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Official Naming
podcast.body: The term "Grunge" gained traction after Bruce Pavitt, co-founder of Sub Pop Records, used it in a label catalog description for Green River's second EP, calling it "ultra-lucy Grunge that destroyed the morals of a generation." "Bruce Pavitt described their second EP in a label catalog as, quote, ultra-lucy Grunge that destroyed the morals of a generation. Unquote, the genre name stuck."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Flannel and Jeans Aesthetic
podcast.body: The grunge look was famously characterized by its casual aesthetic of flannel shirts and jeans. This attire was frequently complemented by black Doc Martens featuring their distinctive yellow stitching, especially prevalent during the early 1990s. "The black boots with their yellow stitching went well with the Grunge flannel and jeans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundation in Drop Tunings
podcast.body: Grunge music emerged with a foundation in "no fingers tuning," specifically drop D or drop C sharp, adopted by guitarists in the Pacific Northwest. This tuning style was directly inspired by Tony Iommi's Black Sabbath guitar sound, which originated from his industrial accident and subsequent modifications. "That dropped D or in Tony's case, drop C sharp became the foundation of grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundation of Commercial Alt-Rock Radio
podcast.body: For many years, grunge became the "foundation" of commercial alt-rock radio's sound. From a ratings perspective, it was safer to play grunge or grunge-ish, guitar-based music, often with drop-tuning, rather than risk chances on truly new and different sounds.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Geffen Records as a Gestational Hub
podcast.body: The grunge movement fundamentally developed at Geffen Records in the late 1980s, making the label a crucial entity for defining the sound of rock in the United States. "en Giffen se gesta el movimiento grancho en los finales de los 80."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Generation X Identity
podcast.body: The key figures of grunge were mostly of similar age, largely belonging to Generation X, described as "the furious generation" and "the first failed generation" in many years, which contributed to its particular character. "el granch está muy delimitado generalmente en lo que conocemos como la generación en X, la generación rabiosa con el mundo un poco, la primera generación fracasada que hayamos tenido muchos años."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Generational Impact
podcast.body: Grunge was Generation X's favorite music and served as a "gateway drug" into many other forms of Alt Rock, leading to movements like the mid-90s punk revival (Green Day, The Offspring), aggressive hardcore and industrial sounds, and an uptick in goth music. "Grunge was not only generation X's favorite music, but the gateway drug into so many other forms of Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Genre Co-option
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, critics and fans identified a wave of "pumped up, dude-bro bands" as Post Grunge, who carried forward the musical mantle established by Nirvana. "a raft of pumped up, dude-bro bands that critics and fans called Post Grunge would carry the mantle of his music forward."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Glory Days as Revivalist Notion
podcast.body: The "glory days of grunge" are currently experiencing a form of rehabilitation or revival, indicative of ongoing nostalgia trends. "the glory days of grunge, even disco has somehow been rehabilitated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Goatee Popularity in Grunge Era
podcast.body: The goatee, a small, trimmed beard, became a highly popular and recognizable style of facial hair during the grunge music era. "There's the whole concept of facial hair, including that little go-t thing that was so big during the grunge era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gone Trend
podcast.body: Grunge is noted as a musical trend and subculture that has "gone," though its echoes persist. "They even grunge as gone, although its echoes remain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge Band Formed in Rehab
podcast.body: Mad Season, described as a "Grunge band," was notably formed at a rehab center when Mike McCready of Pearl Jam met John Baker Saunders. "Next, did you hear about the Grunge band that was formed at a rehab center?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge Invasion of the UK
podcast.body: Grunge, originating from the US, invaded the UK and began to supplant the traditional British rock scene, with American bands like Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and Soundgarden gaining significant traction. "Grunge had invaded the kingdom and was slowly conquering her Majesty's lands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Grunge Overview
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, grunge was a dominant musical style originating from the US, which, along with the punk revival, characterized the American music scene of the time. "The US was mainly about grunge in the punk revival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Guitar Resurgence (1990s)
podcast.body: The emergence of Grunge and the alternative revolution in the 1990s brought about a significant resurgence in the use of guitars in popular music. This period saw a renewed emphasis on guitar-driven sounds after the electronic focus of the 1980s. "Then along came Grunge and the alternative revolution in the 1990s. What did you have? Lots of guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

podcast.title: Guitar Technique Influence
podcast.body: Tony Iommi's pioneering use of lighter strings and downtuned guitar, a direct consequence of his fingertip injury, had a profound impact on guitar playing. This innovative approach contributed significantly to the sonic characteristics and evolution of both grunge and metal genres. "Think about what that little trick meant to everything from metal to grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heaviness and Bleakness
podcast.body: The characteristic "heaviness and bleakness of Grunge seemed a little too much" for audiences following Kurt Cobain's death. This shift in public sentiment led many to seek out lighter, more optimistic musical alternatives. "And suddenly the heaviness and bleakness of Grunge seemed a little too much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Homogenization of Alt-Rock Radio
podcast.body: Grunge's massive popularity effectively turned it into the definition of alt-rock, leading to a homogenization of sound across alternative radio stations. The varied sounds of the 80s were largely squeezed out, replaced by a focus on big guitars and screaming vocalists, as stations looked to national charts for programming cues.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact on INXS Sales
podcast.body: The public's growing fascination with grunge, alongside alternative music, contributed to the underperformance of INXS albums like *Welcome to Wherever You Are* (1992) and *Full Moon, Dirty Hearts* (1993). "A victim of the public's growing fascination with grunge and all things alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact on Music Landscape
podcast.body: The explosion of grunge in the early 1990s led to the complete crumbling of "the walls between mainstream rock and the alternative universe," thereby paving the way for other underground genres like Goth, industrial, various forms of electronica, and punk rock to gain mainstream recognition. "After Grunge blew up in the early 1990s, the walls between mainstream rock and the alternative universe crumbled completely."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Importance of Swans and Sonic Youth
podcast.body: A crucial part of the sound and guitar sounds of grunge, along with other later rock movements, derives directly from Swans, Sonic Youth, and other No Wave bands. "una parte importantísima de su no dio de sus sonidos de guitarra son su ans sonichuth y son todas estas bandas."

podcast.title: Industry Exploitation and Sound-Alikes
podcast.body: Record companies, eager to capitalize on new trends, began signing and marketing alternative groups, leading to an "updraft" that benefited existing bands like Red Hot Chili Peppers and R.E.M., and also propelled new groups, regardless of origin, if they sounded like grunge (low-tuned guitars, slacker heart). "Started signing up and really marketing groups from the alternative side of town."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence and Longevity
podcast.body: Despite its peak lasting only a couple of years, grunge's immense popularity and influence means it has "never really gone away," changing rock forever, even if surviving bands have distanced themselves from the "G-word." "Even though it's peak lasted for just a couple of years, Grunge was so popular and so influential, it's like it's never really gone away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Sonic Youth
podcast.body: The entry of Sonic Youth into Geffen Records led to significant parts of their distinctive guitar sound being incorporated into the grunge albums produced at the label. This cross-pollination enriched American rock, explaining why the guitar sound of the grunge movement sometimes felt very close to Sonic Youth's. "muchísimas partes del sonidjuz se incorporen en los discos de granchos que se estaban haciendo en Giffen."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Influence on 90s Rock Sound
podcast.body: Grunge music significantly influenced the prevalent deep, bass-heavy, and reverbed rock sound of the mid-1990s, notably through bands like Nirvana. "arrastrábamos de las bandas como Nirvana del Grunge."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Queens of The Stone Age  - Villains (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Influence on Britpop
podcast.body: The Britpop scene of the mid-1990s, a nationalistic celebration of British music, was prompted in large part by grunge's popularity, as certain people in the UK were disturbed by the success of American bands with their flannel and detuned guitars. "Consider the Britpop scene in the middle 1990s. That sound, that nationalistic celebration of British music heritage, was prompted in large part by grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Riot Grrrl
podcast.body: The Riot Grrrl movement partly emerged as a reaction against the male-dominated nature of grunge, alongside hardcore, seeking to create music and spaces made by and for women. "Microbands and fans were a reaction to Grunge and Hardcore, yet two more male dominated forms of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Influenced by No Wave
podcast.body: American grunge cannot be fully comprehended without understanding the No Wave movement's redefinition of rhythm, which was often based on noise and distortion. "No podemos entender el granch, no podemos entender el subeis, no podemos entender el trimpob, no podemos entender a my bloody Valentine, no podemos entender al rock industrial, sin entender esa manera, de entender el ritmo casi basada en el ruido y en la distorsión."

podcast.title: Initial Appeal of Relatability
podcast.body: When Grunge emerged in the early 1990s, a significant part of its success stemmed from its performers' efforts to appear as "normal people," mirroring their audience in dress, thought, language, hopes, dreams, fears, and frustrations. This "attitude was really, really important to the success of Grunge." "When Grunge came along in the early 1990s, a big part of its appeal was that the performers on the stage and on the records and CDs tried to come across as normal people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intimate Listening Experience
podcast.body: Grunge, a prominent 1990s genre, provided a distinctly intimate and solitary listening experience. This stood in contrast to Eurodance, which was crafted specifically for mass dancing and shared social enjoyment. "...el Grancho..."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La gran mentira detrás del Eurodance

podcast.title: Lack of Consensus on "First Album"
podcast.body: There is no professional consensus among rock historians on which album marks the definitive start of grunge music or the inflection point between 80s indie rock and grunge. "ni siquiera entre los historiadores profesionales al rock, hay un consenso de cuál es el punto de inflexión que delimita el final del rock indie de los 80 y el inicio del granch."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Leading 90s Music
podcast.body: Grunge music was at the forefront of the "alternative revolution" in the early 1990s, defining a period from 1991 to 1995 with its new and impactful sound. "It's led by Grunge, but supported by all manner of alternative music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Leading Alt-Rock Movement
podcast.body: Grunge was the leading force at the dawn of the 1990s, serving as an "entry drug" that paved the way for the broader alternative rock movement. "Grunge, let the way. But that was just the entry drug."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Local and General Characteristics
podcast.body: Grunge is best defined by two non-musical characteristics: its local origin in Seattle and the general similar age range of its main protagonists. "El granch posiblemente fue un movimiento muy local y muy general, son las dos cosas que mejor delimitan este movimiento."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Longevity of the Scene
podcast.body: Grunge "stayed with us from 1991 through 1995" and continues to be "part of our musical diet," indicating a significant and lasting presence in music history, similar to how Riot Grrrl's impact persists. "Grunge stayed with us from 1991 through 1995, and it's still part of our musical diet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstreaming Alternative Music
podcast.body: The rise of grunge, exemplified by bands like Nirvana, played a pivotal role in making the "alternative world mainstream." This significant shift rendered the term "alternative" confusing, as it was no longer strictly defined by its position outside the mainstream. "So no wonder that many felt that the word was confusing, especially after Nirvana and Grunge made the alternative world mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Massive Production
podcast.body: From its inception, Grunge received immediate and massive production and distribution support from the record industry, distinguishing its rise from the struggles faced by the Shoegaze movement. "que prácticamente meses desde su aparición ya tenían una producción masiva y distribuida."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Mid-1990s Mainstream Dominance
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, the grunge sound, spearheaded by bands like Nirvana and Pearl Jam, dominated radio and television channels such as MTV. "Las radios y los canales de televisión, como MTV, estaban dominados por el sonido granch de bandas como Nirvana y Pearl Jam."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué el cine de los 2000 sonaba así? Big Beat

podcast.title: Mid-90s Loss of Momentum
podcast.body: By the mid-1990s, there was a widespread "feeling that Grunge was slowly losing momentum." Factors contributing to this included Nirvana's In Utero being a sales disappointment and other prominent grunge bands either evolving their sound or appearing derivative, creating an opportune opening for pop punk. "And besides, there was a feeling that Grunge was slowly losing momentum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mixed Feminist Reception
podcast.body: While some parts of the grunge world, and figures like Kurt Cobain and Eddie Vedder, were sympathetic and supportive of feminist causes, the scene largely remained a "boys club," prompting some women to seek their own spaces. "Meanwhile, there was grunge. Parts of that world were down with feminist causes and ideals. For example, Kurt Cobain and Eddie Vetter were pretty woke sympathetic and supportive, but the scene was still very much a boys club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Moist's Embrace of the Wave
podcast.body: Moist, a band formed in Vancouver, successfully "rode the Grunge Wave" of the 1990s with their mid-tempo songs. Their sound resonated well on radio, making them a prominent act within the genre in Canada. "They were formed in Vancouver and rode the Grunge Wave with a series of mid-tempo songs that worked very well on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Moshing Goes Mainstream with Grunge (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Due to the Pacific Northwest's strong punk connections with California, moshing was introduced to the grunge scene. When grunge achieved mainstream success, moshing also became widespread, becoming a standard practice at rock gigs by about 1992. "When Grunge went mainstream, so did moshing. And by about 1992, everybody was doing it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Influences
podcast.body: The sound of grunge was a hybrid, blending hardcore punk and noisy indie with the influences of traditional hard rock bands like Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, and Neil Young. This unique combination resulted in a sludgy, slow, low rock, often as negative and pessimistic as nihilistic hardcore acts, with more introspective lyrics. "No one considered it weird to be into both Black Flag and Arasmith at the same time. And the result was a unique musical hybrid, the product of natural selection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: North American Rise
podcast.body: The rise of grunge and the alternative nation in North America was a significant musical trend, preceding Britpop. "The last show was about the rise of grunge and the alternative nation in North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Nuanced Explosion
podcast.body: Although Nirvana's breakthrough was "seismic," the Grunge explosion's effects on the charts were "more nuanced" than commonly remembered, and alternative rock did not transform into Grunge overnight. "the Grunge explosion had effects on the charts that were more nuanced than we remember today."

podcast.title: Official Start and Trilogy
podcast.body: Grunge officially began between 1981 and 1991, marked by the emergence of the "great Grunge trilogy" featuring bands like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Pearl Jam. "Justo al mismo momento entre el 81 y el 91 arrancaba oficialmente el gruncho, venía la gran trilogía del gruncho."

podcast.title: Origin and Spread – Seattle's Small Beginnings
podcast.body: Grunge began with a small group of perhaps a dozen individuals in and around Seattle. Within a few years, this concentrated scene expanded significantly to become the dominant sound of Western rock throughout much of the 1990s and into the 2000s, requiring a swift and steady chain reaction for its widespread propagation. "Grunge started with maybe a dozen people in and around Seattle. Really, that's it. But within a few years, it expanded to become the dominant sound of Western rock for much of the 90s and into the 2000s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin in Pacific Northwest
podcast.body: Grunge developed in the Seattle area, arising from a crossbreeding of punk and hardcore shows (which were more accessible than major touring acts due to the Rocky Mountains blocking east-west tours) with influences from bands like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Heart. This development would not have occurred without the unique geographical and touring conditions. "And that's how it crossbred with Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath and Hart. To eventually become Grunge, that would not have happened without the Rocky Mountains being in the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins in Pacific Northwest
podcast.body: Grunge emerged in the Seattle area, resulting from a crossbreeding of the punk and hardcore scene (facilitated by touring bands from the West Coast) with influences from hard rock bands like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Heart. The isolation created by the Rocky Mountains, which made East-West touring difficult for smaller bands, contributed to the unique local musical ecosystem. "And that's how it crossbred with Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath and Hart. To eventually become Grunge, that would not have happened without the Rocky Mountains being in the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins in Seattle
podcast.body: Grunge originated entirely within the local Seattle indie scene, seeded by other indie music. Its earliest sounds were captured on compilations like "Deep Six," featuring bands such as The Melvins and Soundgarden. "That's some of the earliest sounds of grunge, arguably the most important alternative sound of the 1990s. And it started in the local Seattle Indy scene. All of it. And it was seeded by other indie music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Over-exploitation and Mythification
podcast.body: By the mid-90s, the grunge movement had been over-exploited and mythified by the music press and record labels. The MTV Unplugged in New York performance by Nirvana helped to unmask the reality behind the movement, revealing disenchanted artists battling severe drug addiction. "la música grancha estaba mitificada."

srcs.episode: Por qué el MTV Unplugged de Nirvana NO es un mal álbum

podcast.title: Overlooked Pioneers
podcast.body: The history of grunge has unfortunately overlooked important and influential figures like Tina Bell and her band Bam Bam, who were "doing the grunge thing" in Seattle as early as 1983. This highlights a gap in the recognized narrative of the genre's origins. "Now this is a sad example of important and influential people being left out of music history."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

podcast.title: Overshadowing Dreampop (1990s)
podcast.body: Grunge is listed as one of the 1990s music styles that gained prominence and began to overshadow Dreampop, leading to its diminished visibility in the mainstream.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pacific Northwest Birthplace
podcast.body: Grunge music originated in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, this area was geographically isolated from major national tour routes, leading to the development of north-south musical trade routes. "Remember that the Pacific Northwest was where Grunge was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pacific Northwest Origins
podcast.body: The genre developed among a small group of musicians and fans in the Pacific Northwest of the United States, in a "petri dish" environment. This unique mix included influences from classic rock like Black Sabbath, Kiss, and Led Zeppelin, alongside hardcore punk from California bands like Dead Kennedys, Black Flag, and Bad Religion, combined with local factors like rainy weather, coffee, drugs, universities, and isolation from major tours. "But something was happening amongst a small group of musicians and fans in the Pacific Northwest of the United States."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parental Connections to Era
podcast.body: A number of the musical offspring discussed have direct parental connections to the original Grunge era. "This last bunch all have parental connections to the original Grunge era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paving the Way for Punk Revival
podcast.body: Grunge's growing popularity helped set the stage for the 1990s punk revival by frequently referencing punk pioneers like the Ramones, The Clash, Black Flag, Buzzcocks, Sex Pistols, The Germs, and Hüsker Dü. This "name-checking" directed new fans to punk's origins. "As grunge grew in popularity, we began to learn more about who influenced these grunge groups. There was a lot of punk name checking going on, the Ramones, the clash, black flag, buzz cocks, sex pistols, the germs, husk or dew."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pessimism Contrasted with Britpop
podcast.body: Grunge was characterized by gloom, pessimism, darkness, and death, which was actively contrasted by Britpop artists like Noel Gallagher of Oasis, who found it annoying. "Compare the optimism found in that song with what was happening with Grunge, all that gloom and pessimism and darkness and death."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Cobain Decline
podcast.body: The death of Kurt Cobain on April 8, 1994, marked the beginning of the end for the recording industry's and the public's intense focus on grunge, creating a vacuum that new punk bands like Green Day were perfectly positioned to fill. "in hindsight, we can see that this event marked the beginning of the end of the public's and the recording industries laser focus on grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prominence in 90s Videoclips
podcast.body: During the 1990s, the musical diversity of the era allowed a wide variety of genres, including grunge, to gain significant presence in the videoclip scene. "Desde el gran y el local alternativo, hasta la música electrónica."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La Magia Perdida de los Videoclips de los 90s

podcast.title: Prominence in Early 1990s
podcast.body: Grunge was identified as "the big thing" in new music during the early 1990s, dominating the musical landscape of the era. "The big thing of course was Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prominent All-Female Grunge Bands
podcast.body: The grunge movement saw the rise of notable all-female bands like L7, featuring drummer Dee Plakas, which demonstrated the growing presence and influence of women in heavy, alternative rock genres. "De Placas of L7, great all-female grunge band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

podcast.title: Purist Backlash and Fragmentation
podcast.body: The mainstreaming of grunge led to an "existential crisis" among purists who questioned what was truly alternative. The inclusion of Metallica on the 1996 Lollapalooza tour exemplified this, causing original alternative fans to lose interest and drift away, marking the beginning of a massive fragmentation of the once cohesive scene. "This caused an existential crisis amongst purists who began to question who and what was truly alternative and who and what wasn't."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Queens of the Stone Age's Stance on the Label
podcast.body: While Queens of the Stone Age denies ever being a "Grunge band," they acknowledge that the genre's popularity and the emerging wave of new metal in the late 1990s and early 2000s significantly influenced their career trajectory. "they are not nor ever have been a Grunge band, although they will admit that they were set on their career trajectory by the popularity of Grunge"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Secrets of Queens of the Stone Age: Part 2

podcast.title: Radio Foundation (Long-term)
podcast.body: For many years, grunge became the "foundation of its sound" for commercial alt-rock radio, leading stations to play "something grunge or grunge-ish" (guitar-based, often with drop tuning) as a safer, ratings-driven strategy rather than taking chances on new and different music. "When it came to commercial alt rock radio, well, Grunge became the foundation of its sound for many, many, many years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rapid Growth and Ethos Shift
podcast.body: Grunge music gained popularity so rapidly that it swiftly shifted the entire ethos of music videos. This genre championed an unpolished and authentic style, rejecting the glamour, fancy sets, and costumes previously common, and promoting anti-fashion and simple camera and band performances. "And because alternative, especially Grunge got so big so fast, the entire ethos of music videos shifted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: Reactionary Nature
podcast.body: Like punk, grunge was a reactionary movement that stripped away the "artifice and goop" attached to 1980s rock, such as elaborate costuming, makeup, and MTV video aesthetics, rejecting the image of rich rock stars with lavish lifestyles. "Like punk, Grunge was reactionary. It was a stripping back of all the artifice and goop that had become attached to rock through the 1980s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relationship to Pop Songs
podcast.body: Grunge, a dominant sound in the 1990s, is described as essentially "Pop Songs with the guitars tuned way low and then turned way up." This interpretation suggests a fundamental pop structure underlying the genre's aggressive exterior, linking it conceptually to Powerpop. "But what was Grunge other than Pop Songs with the guitars tuned way low and then turned way up?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Replacement for Hair Metal
podcast.body: Grunge music emerged in the 1990s, replacing hair metal as a dominant force in rock, alongside other alternative rock styles. "being replaced by grunge in all the Alt Rock in the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reshaping Mainstream Rock
podcast.body: From 1991 to 1993, grunge profoundly reshaped mainstream rock, with bands like Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and Soundgarden selling millions of records and acting as a "gateway drug" to the broader world of alternative rock. "As we brought through 1991, 1992, and 1993, grunge helped reshape mainstream rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise and Dominance in Early 1990s
podcast.body: Triggered by a terrible recession and the First Gulf War in 1990, and the coming of age of Generation X, grunge and alternative music culture rapidly rose to dominance in 1991, clearing out the old guard of pop and hair metal. This music resonated with Gen X's feelings and anger, enjoying widespread popularity until about mid-1996. "In about nine months, the old guard and the pop cohort were cleared out by the rise of grunge and alternative music culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Rise and Dominance in Early 90s
podcast.body: Grunge emerged as a major cultural force in the early 1990s, spearheaded by bands like Soundgarden, Pearl Jam, Alice in Chains, and Nirvana, acting as the initial catalyst for the broader alternative nation movement. "The biggest sea change came with the rise of Grunge, thanks to Soundgarden, Pearl Jam, Alice and Chains, and of course Nirvana. But that music was just the kickstart for the alternative nation that came to dominate most of the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise to Mainstream Dominance (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Grunge emerged as the dominant force in alternative rock by 1992, supplanting the mainstream. Riff-ready songs from bands like Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Alice in Chains, and especially Nirvana, caused alt-rock to coalesce around hard guitar rock. Its immense popularity led to record sales and concert tickets selling in ever-increasing amounts.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Seattle Origin
podcast.body: Grunge was fundamentally a local movement born in Seattle, even though it later conquered the entire United States and the world. Its genesis was strongly tied to two or three independent record labels in Seattle, primarily Sub Pop. "fue un movimiento local de Seattle, el granch conquistó el mundo entero y conquistó Estados Unidos entero pero lo que está claro es que nací en Seattle."

podcast.title: Seattle Origins and Drug Culture (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: The Grunge "explosion" in the early 1990s saw bands like Alice in Chains emerge from Seattle, characterized by their dark themes and the significant role of drugs, particularly heroin, in their music and the lives of their members. "Allison Chains had been one of the first and one of the biggest bands to come out of Seattle during the Grunge explosion in the early 1990s, but they were also one of the darkest drugs, especially heroin, played a huge part not only the band's music, but in the day-to-day lives the guys in the group."

srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Seattle Origins and Unique Scene
podcast.body: Grunge emerged from Seattle, a city distinct from the rest of the West Coast due to its geographical distance from other major American centers, fostering a unique arts and culture scene. Locals consumed rock differently, embracing a blend of traditional hard rock, hardcore punk, and noisy indie influences. "Well, Seattle is in the same time zone as Los Angeles. The city has little in common with the rest of the west coast of the United States. It's not exactly isolated, but Seattle is just far enough away from other major American centers for it to develop a unique arts and culture scene."

podcast.title: Seattle Sound
podcast.body: Seattle's Grunge music was identifiable by its characteristic distortions and heavy bass, contributing significantly to its distinct regional identity and sound. "the distortions and that heavy bass of Seattle's Grunge"

podcast.body: Grunge emerged in the United States between 1989 and 1993, representing one of the two major movements that defined modern indie music, alongside Brit-pop in the UK. "Por un lado sería la música gruncha en Estados Unidos."

podcast.body: The success of bands like The Smashing Pumpkins, which were not from Seattle but had a grungy sound, underscored that Grunge was "a sensibility as much as a scene." This enabled "Grunge adjacent" bands from various regions to dominate charts in 1992-93. "What the smashing pumpkins success reinforced was that Grunge was a sensibility as much as a scene."

podcast.title: Shaping the Grunge Revolution – Butch Vig's Production
podcast.body: The grunge revolution of the early 1990s was significantly shaped by Butch Vig, primarily through his work as a producer rather than a performer. His production of Nirvana's "Nevermind" was a pivotal moment, following his work on Killdozer's "For Ladies Only," which first garnered widespread attention. "Butch Vig a guy who helped shape the whole grunge revolution of the early 1990s Not necessarily as a performer But as a producer."

podcast.title: Unintentional Fashion Style
podcast.body: The distinctive "look" of Pacific Northwest grunge bands, characterized by functional logging industry clothing sourced from thrift shops, was largely unintentional. Musicians couldn't afford the fashionable new wave outfits or the spandex and big hair of mainstream rock, leading them to adopt practical attire. "Most of the members of the music community couldn't afford the cool new wave outfits or the spandex and big hair look of the big mainstream rock bands of the day. They had to settle for the functional logging industry clothing that they could find at their local thrift shops."

podcast.title: Unveiling the Alternative Universe
podcast.body: Grunge "punched a hole" into the parallel universe of alternative rock, which had existed for decades alongside mainstream rock, making its diverse artists and music visible and acknowledged by the general public for the first time. "But grunge punched a hole into this parallel universe, allowing everyone to see what was going on over there."

podcast.title: Vehicle for Mainstream Rock Ideas
podcast.body: Grunge proved to be a "very useful vehicle" that helped "flood mainstream rock with an unbelievable number of good ideas." This era brought about a "vibe change" similar to the punk and new wave era of the mid-to-late 70s, introducing many new sounds and promoting genre mixing. "Grunge turned out to be a very useful vehicle. On mechanism, the thing that helped flood mainstream rock with an unbelievable number of good ideas."

podcast.title: Widespread Saturation
podcast.body: Grunge expanded rapidly from its Seattle origins to become a global phenomenon, leading to a "frenzy and saturation and delusion" where places like Halifax were briefly dubbed "Seattle East" due to the widespread obsession. "that's the kind of frenzy and saturation and delusion that we began to see as grunge expanded from its little corner of America to, well, everywhere."

podcast.title: Woman-Friendly Era
podcast.body: The Grunge era was noted as "one of the more woman-friendly periods of altrock," influenced by the contemporaneous Riot Grrrl movement and the "vocal feminist allyship" of Grunge stars like Kurt Cobain and Eddie Vedder, leading to success for female rockers and female-fronted bands.
